nodes.description: Increased release of EGF-family ligands raises EGFR activity in TOC keratinocytes. Amphiregulin is the ligand that matters for the skin phenotype in mice: deleting it rescues the skin of mice carrying the human TOC mutation. Immortalized TOC keratinocytes have lower total EGFR protein while being more proliferative and migratory, so the signalling change is best described as dysregulated rather than a simple increase in receptor.

evidence.reference_title: RHBDF2 mutations are associated with tylosis, a familial esophageal cancer syndrome.
evidence.snippet: immortalized tylotic keratinocytes have decreased levels of total epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) and display an increased proliferative and migratory potential relative to normal cells, even when normal cells are stimulated with exogenous epidermal growth factor. It would thus appear that EGFR signaling is dysregulated in tylotic cells.

evidence.reference_title: Genetic deletion of amphiregulin restores the normal skin phenotype in a mouse model of the human skin disease tylosis.
evidence.snippet: We generated a mouse model of human tylosis and show that GOF mutations in RHBDF2 cause tylosis by enhancing the amount of amphiregulin (AREG) secretion. Furthermore, we show that genetic disruption of AREG ameliorates skin pathology in mice carrying the human tylosis disease mutation.

nodes.description: A heterozygous germline missense variant in the cytoplasmic N-terminus of RHBDF2. The first variants found were p.Ile186Thr (UK and US families) and p.Pro189Leu (a German family), followed by p.Asp188Asn in a Finnish family, which lies between the two; the Finnish authors suggested that TOC-associated variants may be specific to this site. The variants act as gain of function: N-terminal mutations make iRhom2 more stable, and loss of iRhom2 in mice thins the footpad epidermis instead of thickening it.

nodes.description: Mutant iRHOM2 binds the stress keratin K16 more strongly in TOC keratinocytes. TOC skin has abundant K16 but almost no K6, its usual type II partner, and K16 filaments turn over faster. The authors propose that this K16 axis governs the epidermal response to mechanical stress, which would fit the restriction of the keratoderma to pressure sites; that link is their interpretation.
